Here are the verse-by-verse notes compiled from the sources retrieved:

---

## Numbers 31:28–54 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview of the Passage

This section covers the division of the plunder from the war against Midian, the tribute to the Lord from both the soldiers' and the congregation's halves, and the officers' voluntary gold offering. God himself directed the distribution. (Matthew Henry: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)

---

### v. 28 — "Set aside a tribute for the LORD from what belongs to the soldiers who went into battle: one out of every five hundred, whether persons, cattle, donkeys, or sheep."

- **A tax of one-fifth of one percent**: The tribute ("levy" — literally "lift up" or "heave") from the warriors' half was one soul or animal out of every 500. The NET Bible notes the verb is Hiphil, "you shall cause to be taken up" — a raised offering tax of one-fifth of one percent for the Lord. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=num+31%3A28%2C30%2C33%2C38%2C44)
- Gill says "one soul of five hundred" refers to one woman (person) out of every 500, as the Targum of Jonathan specifies. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)
- Whedon notes this was an acknowledgment of the Lord as the God of battles and author of victory. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-31.html, excerpt)
- Matthew Henry explains that the soldiers were favoured: out of the soldiers' share God required only one in 500, whereas out of the people's share one in 50, "because the people got theirs easily, without any peril or fatigue." The less opportunity we have of honouring God with personal services, the more we should honour Him with our substance. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)

---

### v. 29 — "Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as an offering to the LORD."

- The tribute from the soldiers' half was a **"heave offering"** (or "raised offering") for the Lord, given to Eleazar the priest. Barnes notes the verb from which "heave-offering" is derived is rightly translated "levy" in v. 28, and compares Numbers 18:24. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm)
- Gill says this was "by way of thanksgiving for the success and victory God had given them." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)
- The tribute went to the priests for their maintenance. Whedon adds the priests might put the cattle into their own flocks and slay them as needed; the maidens were employed as servants; the asses they sold. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-31.html, excerpt)

---

### v. 30 — "From the Israelites' half, take one out of every fifty, whether persons, cattle, donkeys, sheep, or other animals, and give them to the Levites who keep charge of the tabernacle of the LORD."

- **One in fifty (two percent)** from the congregation's half went to the Levites. This was a far larger proportion than the soldiers' tribute because (a) the congregation's hazards were less so their gains were less, and (b) the Levites were far more numerous than the priests, so the portion had to be distributed into more hands. (Poole: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/numbers-31.html)
- Gill notes the same reasoning: "the soldiers had taken much pains, and gone through much fatigue, as well as had hazarded their lives, and therefore less was to be taken from them." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)
- Matthew Henry: "the priests were taken from among the Levites, as these soldiers from among the people, for special and hazardous service, and their pay was proportioned accordingly." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)

---

### vv. 31–35 — The Inventory of Plunder

- **v. 31**: "So Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the LORD had commanded Moses" — This phrase appears four times in the chapter (also vv. 31, 41, 47), emphasizing this was the Lord's battle, not Israel's. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)
- **vv. 32–35**: The total plunder remaining: 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 women who had not slept with a man.
- Poole notes "the rest of the prey" means all that was now left; some persons had been killed (v. 17) and some cattle spent for provisions. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/numbers-31.html)
- Keil & Delitzsch argue the numbers are not incredible: judging from the 32,000 virgins, the tribes governed by the five kings may have numbered about 130,000–150,000 people with roughly 35,000 fighting men — easily surprised by 12,000 warriors. The livestock numbers (675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys) are proportionate to a nomadic people. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
- Barnes observes the numbers are in round thousands; hence the Lord's tribute (the 500th part) works out neatly. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm)

---

### vv. 36–40 — The Soldiers' Half and the Lord's Tribute

| Category | Soldiers' Half | Lord's Tribute (1/500) |
|----------|---------------|------------------------|
| Sheep    | 337,500       | 675                    |
| Cattle   | 36,000        | 72                     |
| Donkeys  | 30,500        | 61                     |
| Persons  | 16,000        | 32                     |

- The 32 persons given to the priests were probably "employed as slaves" and used for menial tasks in tabernacle service (cf. Exodus 38:8). (Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/31-28.html; Enduring Word citing Allen: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)
- The numbers illustrate the precision and fairness of God's command. (Matthew Henry: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)

---

### v. 41 — "Moses gave the tribute to Eleazar the priest as an offering for the LORD, as the LORD had commanded Moses."

- This is one of the four "as the LORD commanded" refrains, underscoring faithful obedience in the distribution. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### vv. 42–47 — The Congregation's Half and the Levites' Portion

- **vv. 43–46**: The congregation's half mirrored the soldiers' half exactly: 337,500 sheep, 36,000 cattle, 30,500 donkeys, and 16,000 persons.
- **v. 47**: From this half, Moses took one out of every fifty (6,750 sheep, 720 cattle, 610 donkeys, and 320 persons) and gave them to the Levites.
- The principle of equal division between those who fought and those who stayed was later observed by David (1 Samuel 30:22–25), who seems to have been the first to establish such a rule as a permanent statute. (Peake's Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-31.html)
- Matthew Henry notes that the 12,000 soldiers had as much total as the whole congregation (fifty times as many people), so individual soldiers fared far better — "the greater pains we take, and the greater hazards we run, in the service of God and our generation, the greater will our recompence be at last." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)
- Calvin (on StudyLight) explains: "it would have been a shame that those who remained in the camp should be altogether without any part of the spoil, as if they had been convicted of cowardice, whereas it did not depend on themselves that they had not taken part with their brethren." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/31-25.html)

---

### v. 48 — "Then the officers who were over the units of the army — the commanders of thousands and of hundreds — approached Moses."

- The officers (captains of thousands and hundreds) approached Moses respectfully, calling themselves his servants. Matthew Henry remarks: "the honours they had won did not puff them up, so as to make them forget their duty to him." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)

---

### v. 49 — "'Your servants have counted the soldiers under our command, and not one of us is missing.'"

- **A miraculous preservation**: Not a single Israelite soldier died in the battle. Gill calls this "a most amazing and unheard of thing… not to be paralleled in any history." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)
- Enduring Word (citing Allen) notes: "We have no reason to believe that the protection of the lives of every soldier in the wars of Israel ever happened again. This must have been a solitary act in the history of Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: "A victory so signal, and the glory of which was untarnished by the loss of a single Israelitish soldier, was an astonishing miracle. So clearly betokening the direct interposition of Heaven." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch add that this is not so marvellous as to call the narrative into question; they cite Roman historian Tacitus (Ann. xiii.39) recording a similar event where Romans slaughtered all the foe without losing a single man. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
- One modern commentary (StudyLight, likely Constable) explains that the Midianites were nomads, not a warring people, normally moving on when encountering trouble and were probably caught unprepared. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/31-28.html)
- Matthew Henry draws a Christological analogy: "Of all that were given them they had lost none; so precious also is the blood of Christ's subjects and soldiers to him, Ps. 72:14." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)

---

### v. 50 — "'So we have brought to the LORD an offering of the gold articles each man acquired — armlets, bracelets, rings, earrings, and necklaces — to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD.'"

- **The gold items**: Barnes identifies: "chains" = armlets (2 Sam 1:10), "rings" = finger-rings or seal-rings, "tablets" = ornaments worn suspended from the neck (Exodus 35:22). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch detail: *'es'adah* = arm-rings; *tsamid* = bands/armlets; *tabba'at* = signet-rings; *'agil* = hoops/ear-rings; *kumaz* = gold balls (Exodus 35:22). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
- **"To make atonement for our souls"**: This is a key interpretive question.
  - **Barnes**: The atonement was not for any special offence (which would require blood-shedding), but like the half-shekel at the census (Exodus 30:11–16), was an acknowledgment of having received undeserved mercies. These, if unacknowledged, would have entailed guilt on the soul. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm)
  - **Gill**: It was to expiate any sins they had been guilty of in going out and coming in, "and particularly for sparing the women they should have put to death, for which Moses was wroth with them, Numbers 31:14." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)
  - **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: "It was partly an atonement or reparation for their error (Nu 31:14-16), for it could not possess any expiatory virtue, and partly a tribute of gratitude." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
  - **Poole**: The offering was for their error noted in vv. 14–16 and also as a memorial (v. 54), "or by way of gratitude for such a stupendous assistance and deliverance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/numbers-31.html)
  - **Keil & Delitzsch**: They offered "for the expiation of their souls" (cf. Leviticus 1:4) with the feeling that they were not worthy of such grace — not because they had done wrong in failing to destroy all enemies (contra Knobel). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
  - **Matthew Henry**: "Instead of coming to Moses to demand a recompence for the good service they had done… they bring an oblation to make atonement for their souls, being conscious to themselves, as the best men must be even in their best services, that they had been defective in their duty." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)
  - **Peake's Commentary**: Notes connection to Exodus 30:11–16 — "The offence thought to be involved in taking the number of the people (cf. 2 Samuel 24:1) was perhaps originally due to the feeling that a Divine prerogative had been trenched upon." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-31.html)
  - **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: Simply notes this was "a token of their gratitude for His protection of their men." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-31.html)

---

### vv. 51–52 — "So Moses and Eleazar the priest received from them all the articles made out of gold. All the gold that the commanders of thousands and of hundreds presented as an offering to the LORD weighed 16,750 shekels."

- **The weight**: 16,750 shekels. Barnes estimates the value as about 20,000 British pounds (in his 19th-century context). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm) Jamieson-Fausset-Brown's estimate: £87,869 16s. 5d. sterling (possibly including all the spoil, not just the gold). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm) The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary estimates 16,750 shekels as roughly 6,700 ounces of gold — "over four and a quarter million dollars" at contemporary gold prices. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-31.html)
- Enduring Word (citing Cole): "The total amount of the gold offered by Israel's commanders on behalf of their enumerated troops far exceeded the minimal requirement of one-half shekel per person…. Instead they presented almost 2.8 times the minimal amount." This reveals a generous spirit in the new generation, in contrast to their fathers who perished in the wilderness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 53 — "Each of the soldiers had taken plunder for himself."

- Barnes clarifies: "This verse seems to imply that the soldiers, as distinct from the officers (compare Numbers 31:49), did not make any offering from their plunder." Only the officers brought the gold offering. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm)
- Gill explains that each soldier kept his own spoil and did not deliver it in with the common prey tallied by Moses and Eleazar; yet from that private spoil each contributed toward the freewill offering. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)
- Matthew Henry also notes that the divided portion was only captives and cattle; "as for the plate, and jewels, and other goods, every man kept what he took, as is intimated, v. 50–53." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)

---

### v. 54 — "And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds and brought it into the Tent of Meeting as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD."

- **"A memorial"**: The gold was placed in the tabernacle treasury as a lasting reminder before the Lord. Gill: "in remembrance of the signal victory these men obtained, and of the singular care of divine Providence in protecting them… and to put the children of Israel in mind for their imitation, when favoured with mercies from the Lord." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: It is not said what was done with this enormous quantity of gold. "It may have formed a fund for the support of the tabernacle services during the long years of neglect which followed the conquest, or it may have been drawn upon for national purposes." The word "memorial" (Hebrew *zikkaron*, LXX μνημόσυνον) means "to bring them into favourable remembrance with the Lord" (cf. Exodus 28:12, 29). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
- **Geneva Study Bible** notes succinctly: "that the Lord might remember the children of Israel." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
- Matthew Henry: "a monument of God's goodness to them, that they might be encouraged to trust in him in their further wars, and a monument of their gratitude to God… that he, being well pleased with this thankful acknowledgment of favours bestowed, might continue and repeat his mercies to them." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/numbers/31.htm)
- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds: "The officers' generosity demonstrates a genuine love for the House of God. Christians today should manifest such love for God's House, His Church." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-31.html)

---

## Points of Protestant Agreement and Distinction

The sources consulted show **broad agreement** among Protestant traditions on this passage. No sharp denominational disputes emerged in the search results. The areas of common ground include:

- **Reformed/Presbyterian** (Matthew Henry, Calvin, Barnes, JFB): Emphasise God's sovereignty in directing the distribution, the principle that all we have is from God and subject to His will, and the typological significance of tribute going to priests and Levites.
- **Baptist** (Gill, Garner-Howes): Gill, though a Calvinistic Baptist, reads the passage similarly to the Reformed commentators, with a particular interest in the precise meanings of Hebrew terms. Garner-Howes draws practical application for church giving today.
- **Anglican** (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary): Ellicott provides careful historical-grammatical notes. The Pulpit Commentary notably includes an extended moral-theological essay on the extermination of the Midianites, arguing that Moses acted under the moral sentiments of his age and that God accommodated His guidance to that stage of moral development — a nuanced Anglican treatment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)
- **Lutheran** (Keil & Delitzsch): Take the historical details at face value, defending the plausibility of the numbers and the miraculous preservation.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik): Reads the passage devotionally, emphasising the new generation's generosity, God's miraculous protection, and practical application for believers today regarding gratitude and giving.
- **The "atonement" question** (v. 50): All traditions agree the gold offering did not have expiatory power in the Levitical sense; it was an acknowledgment of unmerited mercy and/or a reparation for the error of sparing the women (vv. 14–16). None treat it as a precedent for purchasing forgiveness.

---

## Modern Scholarship Notes

- **Peake's Commentary**: Notes that the tax of 1/500 for priests and 1/50 for Levites "is not elsewhere mentioned" — it may be unique to this episode. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/numbers-31.html)
- **NET Bible**: The verb in v. 28 is Hiphil ("you shall cause to be taken up"), a technical term for raising a contribution. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=num+31%3A28%2C30%2C33%2C38%2C44)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** engage historical-critical questions about the numbers, defending them by noting that Midianites were nomadic herders, not a warlike people, and could have been surprised and routed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-54.htm)

---

## Catholic and Orthodox Readings

No results were returned from the approved Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) sites specifically on Numbers 31:28–54. The search did not locate relevant pages from these sources within the permitted domains for this passage.

---

## Debated Popular Modern Teaching

No results were found from the permitted sites addressing prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of this passage. However, Enduring Word (broadly Pentecostal-charismatic) does draw a practical application from the officers' generosity: the new generation of Israel "was showing itself to be generous — in contrast to the generation of their fathers that perished in the wilderness." The gold offering "far exceeded the minimal requirement" (almost 2.8 times), demonstrating a willing, grateful heart rather than mere obligation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)
